evidence.quote: Case 1 – A 95-year-old female patient was admitted to our outpatient clinic with a recent diagnosis of AD.
The patient exhibited symptoms including euphoric mood, hyperactivity, pressured speech, hypersexuality, insomnia, agitation, violent behavior, and new-onset alcohol consumption.
Two weeks later, she was admitted to the neurology clinic due to worsening symptoms.

summary.text: 95-year-old woman admitted to an outpatient clinic with a recent diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease and a past medical history of bipolar I disorder that had been in full remission; aripiprazole was stopped three years ago and valproic acid 21 months ago, and escitalopram 10 mg/day had been taken for years.

Euphoric mood, hyperactivity, pressured speech, hypersexuality, insomnia, agitation, violent behavior and new-onset alcohol consumption began six weeks after donepezil 5 mg/day was administered; escitalopram was stopped and olanzapine 5 mg/day was initiated by her psychiatrist (olanzapine at the fourth week after symptom onset), and two weeks later worsening symptoms led to neurology clinic admission; donepezil was suspected to have induced the symptoms and was discontinued immediately.

Workup reported for both patients: flight of ideas, occasional loosening of associations and grandiose content; MoCA 14 out of 30 on admission; Young Mania Rating Scale 46; no abnormalities on physical examination or detailed laboratory investigations; delirium excluded; no fluctuations; Naranjo score 8 (“probable”). No family history of psychiatric disorders.
After donepezil was discontinued, her symptoms fully remitted within six weeks, and mood remained stable with no recurrence of manic symptoms over one year of follow-up.

summary.text: 66-year-old man with Lewy body dementia and hypertension in his history, with no reported personal or familial psychiatric disorders, taking donepezil 5 mg, memantine 28 mg, pramipexole 1.5 mg and rasagiline 1 mg daily for approximately one year.

Pramipexole was reduced and discontinued because of visual hallucinations, which diminished by more than 50% with stable motor symptoms; aripiprazole 5 mg/day was started with further decrease in hallucinations; two weeks later donepezil was increased to 10 mg/day and two days afterward symptoms consistent with mania appeared and progressively worsened.

Presented to the outpatient clinic with elevated mood, increased visual hallucinations, delusions, behavioral disorganization, pressured speech, hypersexuality, insomnia, agitation and increased preoccupation with poetry writing; MoCA 12 out of 30 on admission, Young Mania Rating Scale 40, no abnormalities on examination or detailed laboratory investigations, delirium excluded, Naranjo score 8 (“probable”).

Donepezil was reduced to 5 mg/day, with gradual improvement fully apparent within a few days and no additional treatment needed; mood remained stable with no recurrence of manic symptoms over one year of follow-up.

article_limitations: Brief letter: no tables, figures or supplements; individual laboratory tests, imaging, admission dates and absolute timing are not reported.

Several findings (thought process, MoCA, Young Mania Rating Scale, Naranjo score, examination, laboratory investigations, delirium exclusion, fluctuations and one-year follow-up) are written for “both patients” together; paired values rely on “respectively”.
Causality (donepezil as the precipitating agent) is the author’s Naranjo “probable” assessment (score 8); it is not recorded as definite.

The discussion hypothesis (acetylcholine-serotonin shift, “recurrence of hypomania”) and the 12 previously documented patients are literature/background and are not patient facts; the discussion’s “recurrence” wording is not applied to Case 2, who had no reported psychiatric history.
